content.p: On the evening of Wednesday 17 June 2015, a young white man walked into the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, sat down with a Bible study group for about an hour, and then opened fire on the people around him. Nine Black worshippers died. Dylann Roof, then 21, was arrested the next morning about four hours' drive away. He was convicted in federal court of hate crimes and other offences and sentenced to death in January 2017, and in state court he pleaded guilty and received a life sentence. His convictions and federal death sentence have survived appeal, and he remains on death row in Indiana.
content.h2: A church with a long memory
content.p: Emanuel AME is known in Charleston as "Mother Emanuel". NPR describes it as a congregation formed in 1816, one of the oldest Black churches in the South, which survived being burned down for its part in an 1822 slave revolt. South Carolina Congressman James Clyburn told NPR that this history is why a white supremacist targeted it. CNN noted that, in summer, tourists by the thousands visit historic downtown Charleston and many stop in at the church, so a stranger at the door was not unusual.

Its pastor, the Rev. Clementa Pinckney, had led the congregation for 23 years and sat in the South Carolina legislature for 19, CNN reported. Roof walked in and asked for him. CNN reported that Pinckney brought the visitor into the Bible study shortly after 8 p.m. His cousin Sylvia Johnson told CNN he welcomed the man as "the nice, kind welcoming person he is".

About a dozen people were at the study, according to CNN, among them Tywanza Sanders, his mother Felicia and his 87-year-old great aunt Susie Jackson. The Fourth Circuit, in the opinion that later reviewed the case, put it plainly: the parishioners handed him a Bible and a study sheet, and for 45 minutes he worshipped with them. They stood and shut their eyes for the closing prayer.

Then Roof took out his gun and began shooting. Parishioners dived under tables. The court recorded that he reloaded several times and fired approximately 74 rounds; the account NPR relayed from a victim's daughter, the Rev. Sharon Risher, said 70. CNN, drawing on relatives and on people who had spoken to survivors, reported that he fired from a handgun hidden behind a fanny pack and that .45-caliber casings were found at the scene. The weapon is described differently across the pages. NBC News calls it a Glock 41 bought two months earlier at a shopping mall in West Columbia, while NPR's interview says Glock 45.

CNN's account, based on what relatives were told, says Sanders leapt up and pleaded with the gunman that he did not have to do this. Roof, quoted by Johnson from a survivor, replied with a racist accusation and said he had to do what he had to do. Sanders then tried to shield his great aunt, and both were killed. The arrest warrant said Roof stood over one victim and made a racially inflammatory remark before leaving. According to the Fourth Circuit, he told a woman who was praying aloud to "shut up", asked whether he had shot her yet, and said he would leave her "to tell the story". The Guardian reported that, according to police, three people were left alive so that they could tell the world the killings were driven by hatred of Black people.

CNN's profiles, published within two days, show who died. Pinckney was 41 and a father of two girls. Cynthia Hurd, 54, had worked for the Charleston County Public Library for 31 years. The Rev. DePayne Middleton-Doctor, 49, was an admissions coordinator at the Charleston learning centre of Southern Wesleyan University. Ethel Lance, 70, had been a city worker for 34 years, much of it backstage at the Galliard Auditorium. The Rev. Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, 45, coached speech and track at Goose Creek High School. Myra Thompson, 59, taught Bible study. The Rev. Daniel Simmons Sr., 74, was a church staff member and a former pastor at Friendship AME Church in Mount Pleasant. Jackson, the oldest, had sung in the choir for decades. Sanders, 26, was the youngest.

The wife of Pinckney, Jennifer, and one of their children were in the church office near the Bible study while the shooting went on, NPR reported. Three people survived: Felicia Sanders, her granddaughter and Polly Sheppard.

Roof drove off. The next morning, a North Carolina florist named Debbie Dills was on her way to work in Shelby when she spotted a black Hyundai carrying South Carolina plates and a Confederate flag. She noticed the driver's blond bowl haircut and phoned her boss, Todd Frady, who called the King's Mountain police. Dills followed the car for 35 miles, she told the Guardian, still unsure it was the man police had hunted for 14 hours. Officers arrived within 15 minutes and arrested Roof, who did not resist.

NPR later contrasted the arrest with other encounters between police and Black suspects. Clyburn said the officer who approached the car re-holstered his gun, and the Rev. Kylon Middleton, a lifelong friend of Pinckney, said he was outraged that police brought Roof a meal from Burger King, just two months after a white North Charleston officer shot Walter Scott as he ran away from a traffic stop.

On Friday 19 June Roof appeared by video link before a judge and was charged with nine counts of murder, CNN reported. Relatives of the dead spoke to him. "You hurt a lot of people but God forgives you, and I forgive you," said a daughter of Ethel Lance. Felicia Sanders, who had watched her son die, told the court, "We enjoyed you," and added: "But may God have mercy on you."

BlackPast recounts that funerals followed: Lance and Coleman-Singleton on 25 June at the church, Pinckney on 26 June at the College of Charleston arena, where President Barack Obama delivered the eulogy, three more the following day, and Simmons on 2 July. NBC News recalls Obama describing the victims as "good people, decent people, God-fearing people" and leading mourners in "Amazing Grace".
content.h2: The website and the argument over a label
content.p: On Saturday 20 June a website, LastRhodesian.com, began circulating. It carried a 2,444-word statement and about 60 photographs, more than half of them of a young man the Guardian said was Roof, holding a pistol, burning a flag, or posing with the Confederate flag and at plantation and Civil War sites. The FBI and Charleston police said they were checking whether it was his. The statement spoke of being "truly awakened" by the killing of Trayvon Martin and of searching the web for "black on white crime". It said, "Someone has to have the bravery to take it to the real world." The Guardian observed that it gave no sign of firm ties to any organised white supremacist network.

At trial, FBI Special Agent Joseph Hamski testified that Roof had a Stormfront account under the name "LilAryan", where in the months before the attack he posted messages looking for local people who shared his views, NPR reported.

That same Saturday, FBI director James Comey said he did not view the shooting as an act of terror, defining terrorism as a political act. The remark seemed at odds with the Justice Department's statement that it was examining whether the crime was a hate crime or terrorism, the Guardian noted. CNN called the killings among the worst acts of domestic terrorism in the United States since the Oklahoma City bombing of 1995.

Roof was indicted on 7 July 2015 on nine murder counts and federal charges including hate crimes and civil rights violations, according to BlackPast. Judge Richard Gergel found Roof competent to stand trial about a week before the Guardian's 4 December 2016 report and allowed him to represent himself, a decision the judge called "very unwise", the Guardian reported. Days before the trial, Roof wrote to the judge asking for his lawyers back for the guilt phase only. BlackPast gives the trial's start as 7 December 2016 and says he was found guilty on 33 charges.

The Fourth Circuit's summary lists them: nine counts of racially motivated hate crimes resulting in death, three of racially motivated hate crimes involving attempt to kill, nine of obstructing religion resulting in death, three more of obstructing religion with an attempted killing and a dangerous weapon, and nine firearm counts.

The sentencing phase opened on 3 January 2017. Roof kept his lawyers off the case, he said, so that they would not present evidence of mental illness. "There's nothing wrong with me psychologically," he told jurors. Prosecutor Jay Richardson argued that Roof planned a race-based attack to incite further violence and showed no remorse. Survivors and relatives testified for the prosecution; Hurd's brother Melvin Graham spoke to reporters outside the courthouse afterwards, and Lance's eldest daughter, the Rev. Sharon Risher, took the stand. In a five-minute closing statement Roof told jurors that anyone who thought he was filled with hate had no idea what real hate is. On 10 January twelve jurors, after about three hours, unanimously sentenced him to death, NPR reported. His defense team said afterwards that the case "will not be over for a very long time".

South Carolina also charged Roof with murder and sought the death penalty. NPR's January 2017 report said the state trial, once set for 17 January, had been postponed. He pleaded guilty to the state murder charges on 10 April 2017 in Charleston County, according to an NPR photo caption, and was sentenced to life in prison, NBC News reported. BlackPast's entry says the sentence "was later reduced to life in prison without parole" on that date, which is not what the other pages say: the federal death sentence was not reduced.
content.h2: The gun that should not have been sold
content.p: Families and survivors sued after the FBI disclosed that its background check had failed to catch a fact that should have blocked Roof's purchase. NBC News described the chain of errors: Roof had been arrested on a felony drug charge in Lexington County, and the sheriff's office told the FBI examiner to contact Columbia police. But in the FBI's databases the only department listed was West Columbia's, which had no record of an arrest, and Lexington County had none by that name. The examiner also called the county prosecutor but heard nothing back. Federal law lets a sale proceed after three days if the FBI has not blocked it, and the three-day period expired. Only afterwards did the FBI learn that Roof had in fact pleaded guilty to the drug charge. Then-director Comey said: "We are all sick this happened."

The Fourth Circuit allowed the lawsuits to go ahead, saying the report's information would have been enough to establish that he could not lawfully have a firearm, being an unlawful drug user. On 28 October 2021, the Justice Department settled for $63 million for victims' families and $25 million for survivors, per lawyers involved. Attorney General Merrick Garland called the shooting "a horrific hate crime".

On 25 August 2021 the Fourth Circuit affirmed. Roof had challenged his competency to stand trial, the decision letting him represent himself in the penalty phase, alleged penalty-phase errors, and the constitutionality of some charging statutes. The appeals judges called his argument "strained", held that neither the Constitution nor the Federal Death Penalty Act requires mitigation evidence over a defendant's objection, and wrote: "No cold record or careful parsing of statutes and precedents can capture the full horror of what Roof did." The Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal on 11 October 2022 without comment, NPR and the Associated Press reported. He had asked it to settle how to handle disputes over mental-illness evidence between capital defendants and their lawyers.

Roof is held at the federal prison in Terre Haute, Indiana. NBC News noted in 2021 that Garland had imposed a moratorium on federal executions during a Justice Department review. In April 2025, Live 5 News reported, his lawyers filed a motion of more than 300 pages seeking a new penalty phase. It says his trial counsel ignored expert advice on mental illness, some jurors gave disqualifying answers about the death penalty, and Judge Gergel was biased. It does not dispute that he killed the nine people. Gergel responded that the recusal question had already been dealt with.

BlackPast records that the shooting led the South Carolina legislature to remove the Confederate flag from the state capitol grounds, and that it fed calls to take down Confederate monuments across the country. Five years on, Risher told NPR she was "weary", and Clyburn said the attack "ushered in a re-examination of who and what we are as Americans". Middleton helps run a foundation in Pinckney's memory.
